text: An existing numeric amount field changes from dollars to cents with the same field name and no version or unit marker.
The API now requires mutual TLS certificates from callers that were previously valid using only the documented API key.
An endpoint that previously accepted the documented status value pending now rejects pending and requires queued instead.
A new authorization layer is added. Its effect on previously authorized clients is not described.
A previously optional request field remains optional with the same default; its documentation now includes an additional example.
The old contract guarantees records sorted by increasing sequence. The same endpoint now sorts by decreasing sequence without an option.
The response becomes faster, but a note also says timeouts changed without specifying the values or contract.
The implementation switches database drivers while preserving every public request, response and error contract.
The response previously guaranteed unique IDs across all tenants. It now reuses IDs in different tenants without exposing tenant information.
A response property is renamed, but it is not stated whether that property was part of the public contract or ever returned to clients.
A private internal function is renamed. Network request and response behavior remains byte-for-byte identical.
The API adds a new opt-in version while preserving the current version and its complete behavior for existing clients.
The public response field active changes from Boolean true/false to strings yes/no. Existing valid clients require a Boolean.
The server adds an optional request flag whose documented default reproduces all existing behavior.
A deprecation warning is added to documentation only. The endpoint continues honoring its full published contract.
An endpoint moves to a new address. The note does not say whether the old address redirects or remains available.
A success response changes from HTTP 200 with a JSON object to HTTP 204 with no body. Valid clients are documented to consume the object.
The minimum accepted password length rises from 8 to 12 for an existing API with no version change. Previously accepted 8-character registrations are rejected.
The published list endpoint previously returned every item. It now silently returns only the first 20, and the existing response has no pagination metadata.
The server accepts an additional date format while preserving acceptance and meaning of every previously valid format.
A limit parameter accepts a wider range than before; all previously valid values still produce exactly the same result.
The API adds another accepted enum value; existing request values and every existing response value remain unchanged.
The dependency upgrade says strict parsing enabled. No old or new parsing behavior or public inputs are described.
The old public API allowed a client to retry the same idempotency key and receive its prior result. The new API creates a new payment for each retry.
The response schema is described as modernized, but no field definitions or examples are provided.
The service no longer returns null for a field. The old field contract and replacement value are absent.
A new optional header allows callers to request verbose diagnostics. Omitting it preserves the exact existing response.
A pagination bug is fixed only for inputs explicitly documented as invalid; all valid inputs retain their defined behavior.
Add a new /health endpoint without modifying existing endpoints, authentication requirements or responses.
A documented unlimited string field now rejects inputs longer than 64 characters; longer strings were previously valid.
A signed download link promised to remain valid for 24 hours now expires after 10 minutes, without any change to the requested expiry.
A request body field is removed from examples, but no information establishes whether the server still accepts it.
